components.text: A study of ancient Greece focusing on the brilliant period following the Persian Wars, but embracing as well the formative Bronze, Middle and Archaic ages, and the decline culminating in the conquest of Greece by Philip II of Macedon in 338 B.C.
components.title: University Course Description

components.text:
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
Trace the broad history of Ancient Greece.
Identify the key political, social, economic, and religious innovations of Classical antiquity.
Comprehend how many of these political and cultural innovations shifted over time.
Utilize primary and secondary sources to develop and defend a critical argument about the past.
components.title: Student Learning Outcomes

components.text:
Students will:
Learn how to synthesize and engage with primary and secondary sources for the study of Ancient Greek History through weekly low-stakes assignments.
Write two argumentative essays within the sub-field of ancient history that develop an original thesis.
Be able to recall from memory the key characters, topics, and events that occurred in ancient Greek history before Alexander III the Great's campaigns in the 330s.

Attendance & Participation (20%)
Attendance is mandatory. Please notify me by email before class if you need an excused absence. Students with excused absences will not be disadvantaged, but they must attend office hours to make up missed lecture notes.
Participation includes bringing questions about our readings to class, asking questions during lectures, and being respectful to whoever is talking (both to the instructor and to other students). This includes body language! If you are working with a computer, please be sure to look up from your screen regularly. Students who spend the majority of lecture looking at their screens and not at the board or the speakers will lose participation points.
Weekly Reading Quizzes (10%)
There will be reading quizzes at the start of every class, but only 50% of them (one per week) will count towards your quiz score. The other quiz, called the Check-In, is meant to help you prepare for the exam and maintain a direct line of communication with the professor. Each quiz will consist of one question.
Low-Stakes Assignments (15%)
At regular intervals throughout the semester, I will assign low-stakes assignments that must be completed on Canvas. These will be announced in advance, outlined and discussed in lecture, and due on Friday evenings.
The first assignment is to visit office hours.
Paper 1: Primary Source Paper (10%)
A 1000-word essay is due at the end of week nine. We will work through potential topics, thesis statements, and the paper structure in class.
Paper 2: Secondary Source Paper (15%)
A 1500-word essay is due at the end of the regular lectures. I plan to distribute prompts at the start of week thirteen.
Please notify me before the submission if you would like critical feedback.
Final Exam (30%)
The final exam will be a memorization exam evaluating students’ mastery of the names, dates, places, and important themes of the course.
I will keep a running list of key terms on the board during lectures, and the exam will test students’ knowledge of these terms. A Key Terms list will be distributed to students on the final day of lecture.
The exam will be structured in two parts:
Multiple choice IDs for maps.
Fill-in-the-blank statements for important names, dates, political groups, and places. There will be a word bank for these sections.

components.title: USF Core Syllabus Policies

components.text:
Florida Statute 1004.097 Free Expression on Campus
Students may, without prior notice, record video or audio of a class lecture for a class in which the student is enrolled for their own personal, educational use (USF Policy 10-048). A class lecture is defined as a formal or methodical oral presentation as part of a university course intended to present information or teach enrolled students about a particular subject. Recording class activities other than class lectures, including but not limited to lab sessions, student presentations (whether individually or part of a group), class discussion, clinical presentations such as patient history, academic exercises involving student participation, test or examination administrations, field trips, private conversations between students in the class or between a student and the faculty member is prohibited. Recordings may not be used as a substitute for class participation and class attendance and may not be published or shared without the written consent of the faculty member. Failure to adhere to these requirements may constitute a violation of the USF Student Conduct Code.

components.text:
Students should arrive to class on time and use their computers and devices appropriately. If you have a question about course material, please ask the instructor – chances are other students have the same question.
Students are expected to use non-racist and non-sexist language. Historians often study people and authors who use racially charged or discriminatory language, so it is important that we repeat historical terms and phrases sensitively and with respect and consideration to the victims of the language of the time and our peers in the present. In nearly every case, it is better to use modern terms than risk being insensitive. Please be respectful to each other.
Every student must produce their own work based on their own ideas and cite anyone else’s ideas or words appropriately. If in doubt, always provide a citation! You cannot overcite, and plagiarism, even if unintentional, may lead to serious academic consequences, including dismissal. Expectations on student ethics and integrity are available online: https://www.usf.edu/undergrad/students/ethics-integrity.aspx
Due to the ongoing legal cases over the training data for most LLMs, copying and pasting AI responses qualifies as plagiarism. There is a zero-tolerance policy on plagiarism at USF, and I am required to report any and all cases of suspected plagiarism immediately. Do your own work – I am always amenable to giving extensions, for any reason, so send me an email if you are feeling overwhelmed and need extra time.
You are required to submit a cover letter on every written paper acknowledging how you have engaged with AI. This cover letter does not count towards your word count. You will not be penalized for using AI for revision (this remains a contested point in the Academy – some journals will automatically reject papers that use AI for revision while others are encouraging it), but I will grade you appropriately. Both papers are meant to assess your ability to think critically about primary and secondary sources.
All written submissions should be in formal academic prose. Everyone is strongly encouraged to visit the Writing Studio within the Academic Success Center. Volunteer tutors are available to assist you both synchronously and asynchronously. For more information, visit https://www.usf.edu/undergrad/academic-success-center/writing-studio/
No late work will be accepted, but I am very amenable to offering extensions. If you think you might need an extension or accommodation for any reason, please let me know.
At the very least, students must submit both papers and complete the final exam to receive a passing grade – failure to submit a paper or complete the exam will result in an automatic F.
components.title: Course Policies: Grades

components.text:
The current university policy concerning incomplete grades will be followed in this course.
For undergraduate courses: An “I” grade may be awarded to a student only when a small portion of the student’s work is incomplete and only when the student is otherwise earning a passing grade. The time limit for removing the “I” is to be set by the instructor of the course. For undergraduate students, this time limit may not exceed two academic semesters, whether or not the student is in residence, and/or graduation, whichever comes first. For graduate students, this time limit may not exceed one academic semester. “I” grades not removed by the end of the time limit will be changed to “IF” or “IU,” whichever is appropriate.

components.text:
It is fundamental to the University of South Florida’s mission to support an environment where divergent ideas, theories, and philosophies can be openly exchanged and critically evaluated. Consistent with these principles, this course may involve discussion of ideas that you find uncomfortable, disagreeable, or even offensive.
In the instructional setting, ideas are intended to be presented in an objective manner and not as an endorsement of what you should personally believe. “Objective” means that the idea(s) presented can be tested by critical peer review and rigorous debate, and that the idea(s) is supported by credible research.
In this course you may be asked to engage with complex ideas and to demonstrate an understanding of the ideas. Understanding and engaging with an idea does not require you to believe it or to agree with it.

components.text:
Health and Wellness
Your health is a priority at the University of South Florida. We encourage members of our community to look out for each other and to reach out for help if someone is in need. If you or someone you know is in distress, please make a referral at www.usf.edu/sos so that the Student Outreach & Support can contact and provide helpful resources to the student in distress. A 24-hour licensed mental healthcare professional, offered through the counseling center, is available by phone at 813-974-2831, option 3. Please remember that asking for help is a sign of strength. In case of emergency, please dial 9-1-1.
Title IX Policy
USF is committed to fostering a safe and respectful learning environment, free from sex discrimination and sexual harassment, in accordance with Title IX and USF Policy 0-004. If a student shares an experience of sexual harassment, sexual assault, stalking, or relationship violence with a USF employee (including faculty), that employee will notify the Title IX Office. This allows the Title IX Office to send the student an email with information about support resources and options—if it is safe to do so. Students are not required to respond to this email. The Title IX Office is a private resource. Information is shared only on a need-to-know basis to provide students with support measures. To speak to a confidential resource, students may contact USF Center for Victim Advocacy at 813-974-5757. Confidential resources do not notify the Title IX Office unless the student requests it. For more information about Title IX, available resources, or to make a report, please visit www.usf.edu/title-ix.
Discrimination / Harassment
Discrimination or harassment of students based on protected characteristics is prohibited by Title VI, the Florida Educational Equity Act, and USF Policy 0-007. Protected characteristics include race, color, national origin, shared ancestry, religion, age, sex, disability, genetic status, marital status, and veteran status. If a student shares an experience of harassment or discrimination with a USF employee (including faculty), that employee will notify the Student Equal Opportunity Office. This allows the Student EO Office to send the student an email with information about support resources and options—if it is safe to do so. Students are not required to respond to this email. The Student EO Office is a private resource. Information is shared only on a need-to-know basis to provide students with support measures. For more information about Student EO, available resources, or to make a report, please visit www.usf.edu/student-eo
Course Hero / Chegg Policy
The USF Policy on Academic Integrity specifies that students may not use websites that enable cheating, such as by uploading or downloading material for this purpose. This does apply specifically to Chegg.com and CourseHero.com – almost any use of these websites (including uploading proprietary materials) constitutes a violation of the academic integrity policy.
Professionalism Policy
Per university policy and classroom etiquette; mobile phones, iPods, etc. must be silenced during all classroom and lab lectures. Those not heeding this rule will be asked to leave the classroom/lab immediately so as to not disrupt the learning environment. Please arrive on time for all class meetings. Students who habitually disturb the class by talking, arriving late, etc., and have been warned may suffer a reduction in their final class grade.
Turnitin.com
In this course, turnitin.com may be utilized. Turnitin is an automated system which instructors may use to quickly and easily compare each student's assignment with billions of web sites, as well as an enormous database of student papers that grows with each submission. Accordingly, you may be expected to submit all assignments in both hard copy and electronic format. After the assignment is processed, as instructor I receive a report from turnitin.com that states if and how another author’s work was used in the assignment. For a more detailed look at this process visit http://www.turnitin.com.
Netiquette Guidelines
Act professionally in the way you communicate. Treat your instructors and peers with respect, the same way you would do in a face-to-face environment. Respect other people’s ideas and be constructive when explaining your views about points you may not agree with.
Be sensitive. Be respectful and sensitive when sharing your ideas and opinions. There will be people in your class with different linguistic backgrounds, political and religious beliefs or other general differences.
Proofread and check spelling. Doing this before sending an email or posting a thread on a discussion board will allow you to make sure your message is clear and thoughtful. Avoid the use of all capital letters, it can be perceived as if you are shouting, and it is more difficult to read.
Keep your communications focused and stay on topic. Complete your ideas before changing the subject. By keeping the message on focus you allow the readers to easily get your idea or answers they are looking for.
Be clear with your message. Avoid using humor or sarcasm. Since people can’t see your expressions or hear your tone of voice, meaning can be misinterpreted.
Email and Discussion Board Guidelines
Use the subject line effectively by using a meaningful line of what your email or discussion is about.
Keep your emails and postings related to the course content. You should not post anything personal on a discussion board unless it is requested by the instructor.
Any personal, course or confidential issues should be directly communicated to the instructor via email. The discussion boards are public spaces; therefore, any issues should not be posted there.
End of Semester Student Evaluations
All classes at USF make use of an online system for students to provide feedback to the University regarding the course. These surveys will be made available at the end of the semester, and the University will notify you by email when the response window opens. Your participation is highly encouraged and valued.
Food and Drink Policy (for in-campus sessions only).
Please adhere to the firm policy of no beverages (other than bottled/capped water), food, tobacco products, or like items in the classroom. Your understanding of the necessity for this policy and cooperation will be greatly appreciated. This policy will be strictly enforced.
